chapter_theme: After the council settles that the king should ask about his daughter, he withdraws through a day of palace pool-play, offerings, time-keeping and music, then walks with his guards to the astrologer's mansion, where the astrologer begins to take up the girl's matter.

cast.role: king of the Vidyadharas of the southern ridge, named in this chapter as king of the hill-dwellers (verse 363)
the king's counsellors, who give counsel in the council hall
the women who fan the king and shower him with garlands, like celestial women
the young people who bathe in the palace pools
the women who play in the palace pools and set out offerings
the court's time-keepers who read the water-clock and report the hours
the Vidyadhara guards who surround the king
the astrologer whose mansion the king visits, learned in the book of omens (not the astrologer of the dream in the earlier city)

359.reading: A counsellor says that, by what Satavindu said, the council will learn what is to befall the girl of the yazh-soft voice, while the king stands for the good of the high clan.
359.nuance: The speaker and the one addressed as wearer of the shining thread are not named in the verse; Satavindu is named but his role is left to the sarukkam's earlier verses.
359.event: The council opens on the question of the king's daughter.

360.reading: The others look on kindly and tell the king the matter must be true and he should go to the man's house and ask himself, and the king listens gladly to all they say.
360.event: The counsellors urge the king to go and ask in person, and he agrees.

361.reading: The counsellors tell the Indra-like king to think of nothing else, since delay in counsel hides what is coming, and ask him to enter the palace that touches the sun.
361.event: The counsellors press the king to enter the palace at once.

362.reading: The king sends his counsellors to their homes and walks into the great city's palace past the outer gates, fanned by women like celestials while bees and anklets sound.
362.event: The king dismisses the counsellors and enters the palace.

363.reading: As the king of the hill-dwellers climbs into the hall, the honey-broken, sun-bright rays shine and a ring of light stands in the hall's middle.
363.nuance: Lines 3-4 are compressed; the ring of light is read as a sun-bright disc on the floor.
363.event: The king mounts the radiant hall.

364.reading: Elephants with face-plates, fed cane and betel, ring their bells at their sides while swarms of bees and bangles sound.
364.nuance: The grammar of lines 1-2 is dense; the elephants' feeding is the likely sense.

365.reading: The hall of divine offerings fills with festival: humming bees, honey-dripping garlands, scented paste, offering-banners and singers.
365.nuance: கடவுட் டானம் is read as the place where offerings are made; the compound is not fixed.

366.reading: Young bathers dip in pools of blue lilies and emerald-stepped ponds, and bees fall mingled with the drops.

367.reading: Waves of the lotus-pollened ponds strike the women's breasts, and the pools grow thick with washed face-paste and saffron paste.

368.reading: As women with long hair bathe, they crush the lotus and ambal beds and the bright light of their moon-faces mingles with the water.

369.reading: Women whose kohl has washed off in the great cool pool have eyes as red as long flowers and bow before the lily pollen and honey that spray over them.
369.nuance: The sense of line 3 (hiding from nurses, or the flowers hiding the girls) is uncertain.

370.reading: On wet sand under a pavilion the women hang fans and set up spray from machines, sprinkle sandal drops and paste and scatter blue lilies on the seed-pots.
370.nuance: The device in line 3 is read as a spray-machine; the sprinkling and scattering are the likelier sense.

371.reading: Women like jewelled twigs lay out a flower offering on a gem seat carved to look like a lotus-pod, bright as crystal.
371.nuance: The rare compounds in lines 1-3 leave the exact offering uncertain.
371.event: Women set out a flower offering on a jewelled seat.

372.reading: Skilled time-keepers who know the books of the hours tell the king, at his feet, how many ghatikas have passed and bless him.
372.event: The time-keepers report the passing hours to the king and bless him.

373.reading: With women praising him the king enters his twin-adorned chamber, where he enjoys the nectar to the sound of fine music.
373.nuance: அமிர்தம் can be a drink or simply sweetness; the verse does not say which.
373.event: The king retires to his chamber for music and pleasure.

374.reading: Bright in his white-threaded body and a jasmine garland, the king walks on foot along a street strewn with fresh flowers.
374.event: The king walks along the flowered street.

375.reading: His golden anklets ring, bees and honey-drops follow his garland, and at every step his shark-shaped earrings throw lightning-like gleams.

376.reading: Vidyadhara guards with oiled spears, lances, drawn swords and girded belts close round the king.
376.event: The Vidyadhara guards encircle the king.

377.reading: Women pour garlands and powder over him with folded hands as the king reaches, in his grace, the high gate of the astrologer's mansion.
377.event: The king reaches the astrologer's mansion.

378.reading: The learned man blesses the king as the clan's glory who has come, bidding him take victory, while the auspicious articles are spread.
378.event: The astrologer greets the king with a blessing.

379.reading: The king enters a gem-floored hall thick with aloe smoke and fallen honey as bees hum.

380.reading: Seated in the hall, as the attendants read his sign and leave, the bright-eared one says the matter is the girl's affair.
380.nuance: Which of the two is meant by 'the bright-eared one' turns on the sarukkam's context, not on the line.
380.event: The attendants withdraw and the king states his errand.

381.reading: Bright with bracelet and garland, the astrologer thinks, then begins to speak from his flawless book what he foresees.
381.event: The astrologer prepares to read the omen.

382.reading: Looking at the gold-bright, bending-waisted girl, the astrologer says that the jewelled daughter's matter has come to be weighed.
382.nuance: The verse gives only the opening of his words; the content of the reading is not yet stated.
382.event: The astrologer takes up the king's question.

links.note: Verse 359 puts the question of the yazh-voiced girl's fate to the council, and verse 382 has the astrologer turn to the girl's matter.
links.teaches: The council's question is carried from counsel to omen-reading across the chapter, so a royal question is settled by two kinds of experts in turn.

links.note: The counsellors tell the king to go in at once and not let counsel drag; Kural 638 says a minister must tell even a king who has ruined wise counsel what is good for him.
links.teaches: Here the counsellors' advice is a plain urging of haste that the king accepts, so the Kural's hard case of an unheeding king meets its easy one.

gains.a: A test of what it looks like when counsel is taken without a quarrel, which the verse alone does not discuss.
gains.b: A scene of a minister doing his duty before any failing of the king, which the couplet only imagines after the failing.

links.note: The time-keepers tell the king the hours that have passed; Kural 482 says acting in season is the rope that binds fortune.
links.teaches: The epic shows the machinery of a court that keeps its king aware of the hour, which is what the couplet's rule needs before it can be followed.

gains.a: A reason why a king's day is measured and reported, which the verse treats as ceremony.
gains.b: A working instance of how a king could know the season, which the couplet states only as advice.

links.note: The attendants read the king's sign and withdraw unasked; Kural 701 praises one who reads what is meant before it is said.
links.teaches: The reading of a sign here serves privacy and not counsel, so the Kural's praise of sign-readers is shown at work in a small court habit.

gains.a: A name for the skill of the attendants who leave, which the verse mentions in a clause.
gains.b: A scene where reading a sign is discretion and not advice, a use the couplet does not mention.

links.note: Both epics let the washed-off paste and saffron of bathing women thicken a pool, here in the Vidyadhara palace and there in the city's ponds.
links.teaches: Both Jain epics fix wealth in the cosmetic that the bath washes into the pool, so the image is the genre's mark of luxury.

links.note: The verse thickens a pool with the washed paste and saffron of women's bodies; Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is.
links.teaches: The epic's picture of the bath as pure delight is set against a Jain verse on the same bodies as flesh for vultures.

gains.a: A Jain corrective the poet never voices, so the bath scene stands as one the tradition itself would look past.
gains.b: A scene of the very perfumed bodies the quatrain mocks, shown as the epic's own delight.

links.note: The king ends the day in song and pleasure; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones look to the pain in pleasure and do not cling.
links.teaches: The chapter shows a whole day of enjoyment with no word of its pain, so the quatrain's test of pleasure is left unanswered by the story here.

gains.a: A measure the narrator does not apply, so the night's pleasure goes unjudged in the verse.
gains.b: A king who is shown enjoying, not a fool, which tests whether the quatrain's contrast of wise and foolish fits a ruler.

source_issues: Verses 359-361: the speakers are not named; Satavindu's role and the identity of the man addressed as wearer of the shining thread are given in earlier verses not read here.
Verses 363-371, 378, 380-382: several lines are hard to construe because of the edition's compressed grammar and word division; flagged uncertain.
The king is identified as the Vidyadhara king by verse 363 (king of the hill-dwellers) and by the sarukkam's context; the verses do not name him.
